publisher: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery (2025)
pageTitle: High-rise syndrome in cats (part 2): injury patterns and survival rate
quote: Despite the potential for severe injuries, many cats survive such incidents, thanks in part to the air-righting reflex, an evolutionary adaptation that allows cats to reorient their bodies mid-air to land on their feet.
unsupported: "specialized collarbone", "always land on their feet" (the study found only 3.7% of fallen cats escaped injury), "kicks in within milliseconds"
correctedFact: Cats have an air-righting reflex that lets them reorient their bodies in midair and land on their feet. It is no guarantee, though. In a 2025 study of cats treated after falls from high buildings, only 3.7% survived the fall without any injury at all.
note: Paper also says: "Only 3.7% of the cats in our cohort survived the fall without any injury". No collarbone or timing detail on the page.

pageTitle: Cats can drink cow's milk, TRUE or FALSE?
quote: In kittens, lactase activity decreases after 4 to 7 weeks [1]. ... All cats are lactose intolerant, it's just a matter of quantity! In the study mentioned above, cats tolerated 1.3g of lactose per kilo but not 4.5g/kg. It is the state of the stools that informs us about their tolerance. If your cat has diarrhea when drinking milk, it means that it does not tolerate it.
unsupported: "Skip the milk bowl": the veterinary nutritionist says most adult cats can digest a small amount of milk
correctedFact: Kittens' lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, drops off between 4 and 7 weeks of age. Most adult cats can still handle a small amount of milk, but a bigger dose brings diarrhea, so a cat with loose stools after milk is telling you it does not tolerate it.
note: Owner's eye: the source contradicts the card's advice to skip milk entirely; it says a small, diluted amount is fine for most adult cats.

pageTitle: 4 reasons why your furry feline snoozes most of the day
quote: Cats are crepuscular, which means they are most active during low light times of day, including dawn and dusk, says Alison Meindl, DVM, DABVP, veterinarian and assistant professor at the Colorado State University Veterinary Teaching Hospital.
unsupported: "up to 70% of their lives sleeping", "conserve energy the rest of the time"
correctedFact: Cats are crepuscular, which means they are most active during the low light times of day: dawn and dusk. So the cat that tears around the house at sunrise or sunset is not being strange. It is simply keeping the schedule its body is built for.
note: Owner's eye: the 70% figure (the card's title) traced only to pet sites; one search found it may come from a shelter study where 70% was time alert, not asleep. Second search for a credible lifetime sleep figure found none.

pageTitle: Prevalence and risk factors for feather-damaging behavior in psittacine birds: Analysis of a Japanese nationwide survey
quote: The causes of FDB have been reported to have origins in boredom ..., environmental stress ..., loneliness (e.g., social isolation, absence of the preferred owner) [7, 20, 21], separation anxiety [7, 9, 22] ... We focused on how the presence of humans, conspecific cage mates, and other birds or animals affects FDB because parrots are highly social animals [9, 25]. ... Species, bird age and signs of separation anxiety were significantly higher risk factors for feather-damaging behavior than any other potential risk factors.
unsupported: "need social interaction daily", "highly intelligent birds that thrive on engagement"
correctedFact: Parrots are highly social, and loneliness is one of the reported causes of feather plucking. A 2021 survey covering 2,331 pet parrots in Japan found that birds showing signs of separation anxiety when their owner left home were at significantly higher risk of damaging their own feathers.
note: Same study found time left with no human present did not itself change the odds; separation anxiety did.

pageTitle: Pet rabbits need freedom to exercise, study finds
quote: The researchers suggest this activity rebound demonstrates the rabbits' need to move every day, and their welfare is compromised when they can only do so at midday.
unsupported: "at least 3 hours of exercise": in the study, three hours of run access at midday was the restricted condition that raised stress, not a recommended minimum; "not low-maintenance pets"
correctedFact: Rabbits need room to move every day. In a University of Bristol study, pairs allowed into their run for only three hours at midday burst into play once released and, in small hutches, had the highest stress hormone levels. The researchers concluded their welfare suffers under that routine.
note: Owner's eye: the card's 3 hour minimum is a pet-site figure and runs against this study, which found 3 hours at midday was not enough.

pageTitle: Guinea Pig (Cavia porcellus) Welfare: Associations Between Husbandry Practices, Human-Animal Interactions, and Animal Behaviour
quote: However, individual housing must be avoided due to the highly social nature of guinea pigs [5, 15, 17], and it is legally prohibited in such countries as Austria [18] and Switzerland [19].
unsupported: "lonely, anxious, and even depressed"
correctedFact: Guinea pigs are highly social, and researchers say keeping one alone must be avoided. It is even illegal in Austria and Switzerland. Experts recommend at least three, so that if a companion dies the survivor is not left completely alone while a new friend is slowly introduced.
note: Paper also: "These findings support the recommendation by guinea pig experts to keep at least three animals, reducing the likelihood that one animal will be left alone if a companion passes away".

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
pageTitle: National Zoo Mourns Loss of Aldabra Tortoise and Wrinkled Hornbill
quote: Aldabra tortoises have extraordinary long lifespans, and can live for more than 100 years. Keepers estimate that Sable was at least 87 years old and possibly could have been closer to 100 years old
unsupported: "Tortoises" in general (the source covers Aldabra giant tortoises); "You may need to include them in your will!" is advice, not a sourced claim
correctedFact: Aldabra giant tortoises can live for more than 100 years. At the Smithsonian's National Zoo, a female named Sable arrived in 1956 as an adult at least 30 years old, and keepers estimated she was at least 87 when she died, possibly closer to 100.
note: Most pet tortoise species are not giant tortoises, so the generic "tortoises" wording overreaches.

pageTitle: Largest vocabulary for a bird ever
quote: The bird with the largest vocabulary was a budgerigar, Puck, owned by Camille Jordan of Petaluma, California, USA, who knew an estimated 1728 words before its death in 1994.
unsupported: "Many parrots can mimic not just single words but full sentences, tones, and even laughs"
correctedFact: The record for the largest vocabulary of any bird does not belong to a big exotic parrot. Guinness World Records credits it to Puck, a budgerigar owned by Camille Jordan of Petaluma, California, who knew an estimated 1,728 words before its death in 1994.
extraPoints: Many parrots mimic full sentences, tones and laughs, not just single words
note: Core record confirmed word for word; only the general lead-in is unsourced.

publisher: University of Texas Marine Science Institute
pageTitle: Ampullae of Lorenzini
quote: The network consists of hundreds or thousands of pores on the shark's head that are big enough to see with the naked eye. ... Each canal leads to a small gel-filled chamber — the ampulla — that's lined with nerve cells. These organs detect the electrical impulses generated by the muscle contractions of nearby fish, seals, or other creatures. They're so sensitive that they can even detect a beating heart. But they only work at close range — within a few inches.
unsupported: "from over a meter away" (the source says within a few inches)
correctedFact: Sharks have hundreds or thousands of pores on their heads, called ampullae of Lorenzini, that lead to gel-filled chambers lined with nerve cells. They sense the tiny electrical impulses from the muscles of nearby animals and can even detect a beating heart, but only within a few inches.
note: Owner's eye: the card's range is contradicted, not just unsourced.

publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2004)
pageTitle: The crafting of hook tools by wild New Caledonian crows
quote: New Caledonian crows manufacture an impressive range of stick and leaf tools. We previously reported that their toolkit included hooked implements made from leafy twigs, although their manufacture had never been closely observed. We describe the manufacture of 10 hooked-twig tools by an adult crow and its dependent juvenile.
unsupported: "to extract grubs from bark", "they pass these techniques on to their young, making it a form of animal culture"
correctedFact: New Caledonian crows craft hooked tools from leafy twigs in three steps: choosing the raw material, trimming it, then carefully sculpting the hook. Researchers watched an adult crow and its dependent juvenile make 10 of these tools in the wild, a level of crafting not seen in chimpanzees' wooden tools.
note: Abstract also: "Hooked-twig manufacture contrasts with the lack of sculpting in the making of wooden tools by other non-humans such as chimpanzees and woodpecker finches." First try (Hunt and Gray 2003, PMC1691310) only had an abstract on pandanus tools.

pageTitle: Hippos beat the burn
quote: Researchers have identified the chemicals responsible for the ancient myth that the beasts sweat blood. In reality, hippos' secretions are neither blood nor precisely sweat, but a mixture of pigments that function as both sunscreen and antibiotic, as well as keeping the animals cool
unsupported: "Scientists once thought it was blood" (the source calls it an ancient myth), "oily", "earning it the nickname 'blood sweat'"
correctedFact: Hippos ooze a blood red secretion behind the ancient myth that they sweat blood. It is neither blood nor true sweat. Its red and orange pigments block harmful ultraviolet rays like a sunscreen, and the red one also holds back the growth of disease-causing bacteria.
note: Reports Saikawa et al., Nature 429:363 (2004).

pageTitle: Ants Farmed Fungi in the Wake of Dinosaurs' Demise 66 Million Years Ago
quote: Leafcutter ants today, for example, snip off leaves to take back to their nests and deposit them as food for the fungus that they then eat. ... Agricultural ants evolved about 66.65 million years ago, the researchers found
unsupported: "They've been farming for over 50 million years": the 66 million year date is for fungus-farming ants as a group; the same Smithsonian research says leafcutters' advanced farming came roughly 40 million years later
correctedFact: Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they carry. They snip them off and haul them home as food for a fungus, and the fungus is what they eat. Ants have been farming fungi for about 66 million years, since the asteroid strike that doomed the dinosaurs.
note: Smithsonian newsroom release blocked automated fetch; magazine article read via WebFetch. Covers Schultz et al., Science (2024).

pageTitle: Mirror self-recognition in the bottlenose dolphin: A case of cognitive convergence
quote: The ability to recognize oneself in a mirror is an exceedingly rare capacity in the animal kingdom. To date, only humans and great apes have shown convincing evidence of mirror self-recognition. Two dolphins were exposed to reflective surfaces, and both demonstrated responses consistent with the use of the mirror to investigate marked parts of the body.
unsupported: "and elephants" (not in this 2001 paper, which lists elephants among species with no convincing evidence at the time), "a sense of self-awareness" (the authors say deeper self-awareness remains unanswered)
correctedFact: Bottlenose dolphins pass the mirror test. In a 2001 study, two dolphins used a mirror to inspect marks placed on their bodies. It was the first convincing evidence of mirror self-recognition outside humans and great apes, a capacity the researchers called exceedingly rare in the animal kingdom.
note: Elephants were shown later (Plotnik et al. 2006), so the card is not wrong, but this source does not carry that word.

pageTitle: WATCH: This bird can stay ten months in the air without landing!
quote: Using a new type of microdata log, the researchers at the Faculty of Science in Lund have managed to prove that the common swift only lands for two months of the year, during the breeding season. The rest of the time, ten months, they spend in the air
unsupported: "They eat, sleep, and even mate in the sky" (the source says how they sleep is still unknown and does not mention mating)
correctedFact: Common swifts can stay in the air for ten months straight. Lund University researchers tracked 13 birds with data loggers: some never landed once in that time, and even those that did spent more than 99.5% of it airborne. They land only during the two month breeding season.
note: Paper: Hedenstrom et al., Current Biology (2016); journal page blocked automated fetch. Lund quote on sleep: "Perhaps they sleep during a declining glide, but we're not sure".

pageTitle: Shrimps spew bubbles as hot as the sun
quote: While earlier experiments had shown that so-called snapping shrimp generate imploding air bubbles that make loud popping sounds (SN: 9/23/00, p. 199), a new study reveals that those collapsing bubbles emit flashes of light and may flare as hot as the sun's surface. ... The animals use snaps to fight rivals, find mates, and even stun prey.
unsupported: "or kills prey instantly"
correctedFact: When a pistol shrimp slams its claw shut, it makes a bubble that collapses with a loud pop and a flash of light, and that bubble may flare as hot as the surface of the sun. Snapping shrimp use their snaps to fight rivals, find mates and even stun prey.
note: Reports Lohse et al., Nature (2001). First try (University of Twente Physics of Fluids page) would not load.

pageTitle: Zebra
quote: Zebra stripes are unique to each individual—a fact that helps researchers identify individual zebras. ... Foals must recognize their mother from birth to survive. A foal learns its mother's stripe pattern to stay close to her.
unsupported: "like a fingerprint", "by their stripe pattern alone", "within hours of being born"
correctedFact: Every zebra's stripe pattern is unique to that individual, which is how researchers can tell one zebra from another. A newborn foal puts that to use too: it learns its mother's stripe pattern so it can stay close to her, since mares usually do not adopt other foals.
extraPoints: Foals recognize their mothers by her stripe pattern
note: Page also says mothers separate from the herd so foals can imprint on them.

pageTitle: Flawed analysis invalidates claim of a strong Yellowstone trophic cascade after wolf reintroduction: A comment on Ripple et al. (2025)
quote: Ripple et al. (2025) recently argued that large carnivore recovery in Yellowstone National Park triggered one of the world's strongest trophic cascades, citing a ~1500% increase in willow crown volume derived from plant height data. In this comment, we show that their conclusion is invalid due to fundamental methodological flaws. ... These shortcomings explain the apparent conflict with Hobbs et al. (2024), who found evidence for a relatively weak trophic cascade
unsupported: "in 1995", "elk behavior changed", and the river framing: the 2025 re-analysis is about willow regrowth, not the claim that wolves reshaped the park's rivers
correctedFact: After wolves returned to Yellowstone, a 2025 study claimed willows had rebounded by about 1,500%, one of the world's strongest trophic cascades. Researchers from Utah State and Colorado State answered that the claim rests on flawed methods, and that the evidence points to a relatively weak cascade.
note: Owner's eye: the card ties the 2025 re-analysis to the rivers story, but the paper critiques a willow study. Text read from the authors' EcoEvoRxiv preprint (doi 10.32942/x2qq0c); published version is the DOI given. Quote checked against the preprint text with its line numbers removed.

pageTitle: Cranial Appendages in Ruminants: Diversity, Evolution, Development, and Molecular Basis of Horns, Pronghorns, Antlers, and Ossicones
quote: During their development, antlers are highly vascularized, possess significant sensory innervation, and are the fastest-growing tissue in animals, with growth rates exceeding 2 cm per day [41, 49].
unsupported: "up to an inch per day" (source: more than 2 cm, about 0.8 inch), "covered in 'velvet,' a soft skin", "until they harden each autumn"
correctedFact: Deer antlers are the fastest-growing tissue in animals, adding more than 2 centimeters, about 0.8 inch, a day. While they grow, antlers are packed with blood vessels and nerves, and that rich blood supply fuels the rapidly multiplying cartilage cells at their tips.
note: First two tries (Animal Production Science review, Te Ara) blocked automated fetch; this open-access review was the replacement.

pageTitle: Orange Clownfish
quote: They are protandrous hermaphrodites, which means all fish are males except for the largest of the group, which is female. Once the female dies, the largest male becomes female, and the others move up the hierarchy.
unsupported: "permanently", "Finding Nemo got it backwards!"
correctedFact: Clownfish are protandrous hermaphrodites: every fish develops into a male first, and only the largest in the group is female. When that female dies, the largest male becomes the new female, and every fish below moves up one place in the group's strict pecking order.
note: Page also: "Anemonefishes are characterized by being protandrous hermaphrodites which means that all fish develop into males first".

publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2021)
pageTitle: Electrostatic resistance to alpha-neurotoxins conferred by charge reversal mutations in nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
quote: By contrast, the evolution of 187R in the honey badger has only been hypothesized to confer resistance to α-neurotoxins [4], due to them being predators of cobras (Naja) and based on natural history observations of them surviving cobra bites [4, 18]. ... As expected, the native state was not bound by the three sympatric cobra venoms tested
unsupported: "nearly immune", "filmed getting bitten by cobras, going limp for a few minutes, then waking up and continuing to eat the snake"
correctedFact: Honey badgers hunt cobras, and naturalists have long seen them survive cobra bites. A 2021 study found part of the reason: the nerve receptor that cobra neurotoxins attack carries a single amino acid change in honey badgers, and three cobra venoms tested failed to bind to it.
note: The famous limp-then-recover scene is from wildlife TV, not a paper.

pageTitle: Superb Lyrebird
quote: About 80% of the song consists of expert mimicry, with both and joined together in a rousing medley. Sounds can include anything heard in the bird's immediate surroundings, such as chainsaws, car engines, dog barks and local native birds.
unsupported: "perfectly mimic almost any sound", "car alarms, camera shutters", "human voices", "recorded mimicking entire construction sites"
correctedFact: About 80% of the superb lyrebird's song is expert mimicry. It stitches together sounds from its surroundings, from local native birds and dog barks to car engines and chainsaws, into one rousing medley, alongside its own whistles, cackling notes and a loud alarm shriek.
note: The page's sentence is garbled as published ("with both and joined together").

pageTitle: Cuttlefish 'mesmerise' their prey with a moving skin pattern, study finds
quote: the team uncovered a novel form of motion camouflage, whereby the broadclub cuttlefish pass dark stripes downwards across their head and arms to disguise their hunting manoeuvres. ... Their findings suggest that the visual system of the prey may be overwhelmed by the strong motion produced by the stripes, causing them to fail to detect the looming cues of the approaching predator.
unsupported: "hypnotize", "freezes crabs and shrimp in place", "dazzling light show", "at high speed"
correctedFact: Broadclub cuttlefish hunt with a moving skin display, rippling dark stripes down their head and arms in the last moments of their approach. A 2025 University of Bristol study found the motion seems to overwhelm a crab's vision, so it fails to notice the predator looming closer.
note: The study frames it as motion camouflage that hides the approach, not as freezing prey.

publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2001)
pageTitle: Dynamic mimicry in an Indo-Malayan octopus
quote: We observed nine individuals of this species displaying a repertoire of postures and body patterns, several of which are clearly impersonations of venomous animals co-occurring in this habitat. ... our observations suggest that the octopus makes decisions about the most appropriate form of mimicry to use, allowing it to enhance further the benefits of mimicking toxic models by employing mimicry according to the nature of perceived threats.
unsupported: "over 15 different species", "lionfish, flatfish, and sea snakes" (not in the abstract), "changing color in real time"
correctedFact: The mimic octopus forages on open sand in broad daylight, in full view of predatory fish. It shifts between postures and body patterns that clearly impersonate venomous animals living nearby, and researchers who filmed it in Indonesia think it chooses which impersonation to use depending on the threat.
note: Only the abstract is machine-readable (full text is a scanned PDF). Second try, the AMNH mimic octopus page, blocked fetch. The 15 species figure traced only to popular sites.

pageTitle: Expression of Opsins of the Box Jellyfish Tripedalia cystophora Reveals the First Photopigment in Cnidarian Ocelli and Supports the Presence of Photoisomerases
quote: Cubomedusae, or box jellyfish, have a complex visual system comprising 24 eyes of four types. ... These image-forming eyes, the upper and lower lens eyes, share many structural similarities with vertebrate camera-type eyes such as a hemisphere-shaped retina made of ciliary photoreceptors, a single spherical lens at least partly focusing the light onto the retina, and an adjustable pupil in the lower lens eye
unsupported: "they can see in full color" (contradicted: the paper cites Garm et al. 2007, "The lens eyes of the box jellyfish ... are slow and color-blind"), "arranged in four clusters", "having no brain"
correctedFact: Box jellyfish have 24 eyes of four different types. Two of them, the upper and lower lens eyes, form images and share many features with our own camera-type eyes: a hemisphere-shaped retina, a single spherical lens that focuses light, and, in the lower lens eye, an adjustable pupil.
note: Owner's eye: the full color claim is wrong; the lens eyes use a single opsin and are thought to be color-blind.

pageTitle: Goat kids develop accents
quote: But the calls of kids raised in the same social groups were also similar to each other, and became more similar as the kids grew older. This suggests that goat kids modify their calls according their social surroundings, developing similar 'accents'.
unsupported: "regional" (the accents are shared within social groups, not regions)
correctedFact: Goat kids develop accents. Researchers at Queen Mary University of London found that pygmy goat kids raised in the same social group came to sound more alike as they grew older, a sign of vocal flexibility in mammals whose calls were long thought to be genetically fixed.
note: Study: Briefer and McElligott, Animal Behaviour (2012). Release: "in most other mammals (except, for example, bats and whales) vocalisations were thought to be genetically determined".
